concepts.d: Branch of the left coronary artery that descends in the anterior interventricular groove. It supplies the anterior surface of both ventricles and the anterior 2/3 of the septum. The coronary arteries supply the myocardium itself; their obstruction causes ischaemia and infarction.

concepts.n: Circumflex branch of the left coronary artery
concepts.d: It runs in the left coronary groove to the posterior surface of the heart and supplies the atrium and the lateral wall of the left ventricle. The coronary arteries supply the myocardium itself; their obstruction causes ischaemia and infarction.
Branch of the celiac trunk that runs along the lesser curvature of the stomach and gives off oesophageal branches.

concepts.n: Inferior lobe of the left lung
concepts.d: Lobe below the oblique fissure of the left lung; it forms most of the diaphragmatic and posterior surfaces. The lungs contain ≈300–500 million alveoli, with an exchange surface of ≈70 m².

concepts.n: Inferior lobe of the right lung
concepts.d: Basal and posterior lobe of the right lung, below the oblique fissure. It has five segments (superior and four basal). The lungs contain ≈300–500 million alveoli, with an exchange surface of ≈70 m².

Branch of the right coronary artery that descends along the right (acute) margin of the heart and supplies the right ventricle. The coronary arteries supply the myocardium itself; their obstruction causes ischaemia and infarction.

concepts.n: Middle lobe of the right lung
concepts.d: Lobe exclusive to the right lung, bounded by the horizontal and oblique fissures. It has two segments: lateral and medial. The lungs contain ≈300–500 million alveoli, with an exchange surface of ≈70 m².

It descends in the posterior interventricular groove and supplies the posterior third of the septum and the inferior surface of the ventricles. It arises from the right coronary artery in ≈80 % of people (right dominance). The coronary arteries supply the myocardium itself; their obstruction causes ischaemia and infarction.

concepts.n: Posterior papillary muscle of the left ventricle
concepts.d: Projection of the left ventricular myocardium attached by chordae tendineae to the cusps of the mitral valve. It prevents their prolapse during systole.

concepts.n: Posterior papillary muscle of the right ventricle
concepts.d: Projection of the right ventricular myocardium attached by chordae tendineae to the tricuspid valve. It prevents their prolapse during systole.

Terminal branch of the right coronary artery that supplies the posterolateral surface of the left ventricle. The coronary arteries supply the myocardium itself; their obstruction causes ischaemia and infarction.

concepts.n: Septal branches of the left coronary artery
concepts.d: Branches of the anterior interventricular artery that penetrate the anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum, where the conduction system runs. The coronary arteries supply the myocardium itself; their obstruction causes ischaemia and infarction.

concepts.n: Septal branches of the right coronary artery
concepts.d: Small branches that penetrate the posterior third of the interventricular septum. The coronary arteries supply the myocardium itself; their obstruction causes ischaemia and infarction.

concepts.n: Posterior veins of the left ventricle
concepts.d: They drain the diaphragmatic surface of the left ventricle into the coronary sinus.

It arises from the left aortic sinus and, after a short course (≈1 cm), divides into the anterior interventricular and circumflex branches. The coronary arteries supply the myocardium itself; their obstruction causes ischaemia and infarction.

It arises from the right aortic sinus and runs in the right coronary groove. It supplies the right atrium and ventricle and, in most people, the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes. The coronary arteries supply the myocardium itself; their obstruction causes ischaemia and infarction.

concepts.n: Superior lobe of the left lung
concepts.d: Upper lobe of the left lung. It includes the lingula, equivalent to the right middle lobe, and the cardiac notch that leaves room for the heart. The lungs contain ≈300–500 million alveoli, with an exchange surface of ≈70 m².

concepts.n: Superior lobe of the right lung
concepts.d: Apical lobe of the right lung, separated from the middle lobe by the horizontal fissure. It has three segments: apical, posterior and anterior. The lungs contain ≈300–500 million alveoli, with an exchange surface of ≈70 m².
Skeletal muscle. It adducts and lowers the arm.
Skeletal muscle. It abducts and flexes the fifth toe.
Skeletal muscle. It abducts the little finger.
Skeletal muscle. It abducts and flexes the big toe; it supports the medial arch.
Skeletal muscle. It abducts the thumb.
Skeletal muscle. It abducts and extends the thumb.

concepts.n: Accessory short gyrus of the insula
concepts.d: Gyrus of the cerebral cortex (grey matter). Small gyrus of the anterior part of the insula.
Skeletal muscle. It abducts the arm (from 15° to 90°, after initiation by the supraspinatus).
Skeletal muscle. It adducts the thigh.
Skeletal muscle. It adducts the thigh.
The largest of the adductors; between its insertions it leaves the adductor hiatus, through which the femoral vessels pass to the popliteal fossa.
Upper portion, often separate, of the adductor magnus.
Gland located on the upper pole of each kidney. The cortex produces cortisol, aldosterone and androgens; the medulla, adrenaline and noradrenaline.
Almond-shaped group of nuclei in the anterior part of the temporal lobe. It processes emotions, especially fear, and assigns emotional value to memories.
Skeletal muscle. It helps extend the elbow and stabilises the joint.
Gyrus of the cerebral cortex (grey matter). It surrounds the end of the superior temporal sulcus. In the dominant hemisphere it is key for reading, writing and calculation.
Skeletal muscle. It depresses the mandible and elevates the hyoid.
Bundle of fibres that crosses the midline in front of the fornix; it connects the temporal lobes and olfactory structures of both hemispheres.
Sheet of white matter between the caudate nucleus and the lentiform nucleus. It contains fibres between the thalamus and the frontal cortex and frontopontine fibres.

concepts.n: Anterior papillary muscle of the right ventricle
concepts.d: Conical projection of the ventricular myocardium attached to the cusps by the chordae tendineae. By contracting in systole it prevents the atrioventricular valve cusps from bulging back into the atrium.
Gyrus of the cerebral cortex (grey matter). Its upper surface contains the primary auditory cortex (transverse gyri of Heschl).
Tough tendinous sheet that covers the cranial vault and joins the frontal and occipital bellies of the occipitofrontalis muscle. It is firmly attached to the skin of the scalp.
Narrow blind diverticulum (≈8 cm) that arises from the caecum. Rich in lymphoid tissue. Its inflammation (appendicitis) is the most frequent abdominal surgical emergency.
Curved portion of the aorta over the left main bronchus. The brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid and the left subclavian arise from it.
First segment of the aorta, from the aortic valve to the arch (≈5 cm). The coronary arteries arise from its root.
Skeletal muscle. It lowers the scapula and helps its upward rotation.

First cervical vertebra. It has no body or spinous process: it is a ring with two lateral masses that support the skull. The atlanto-occipital joint allows flexion and extension of the head ("saying yes").
Second cervical vertebra. Its dens (odontoid process) acts as a pivot around which the atlas turns: the atlantoaxial joint allows rotation of the head ("saying no").
Central and longest portion of the sternum. The 2nd to 7th costal cartilages articulate with its lateral borders.
Skeletal muscle. Main flexor of the elbow in any position of the forearm.
First and largest branch of the aortic arch. After the right sternoclavicular joint it divides into the right common carotid and subclavian arteries.
Formed by the union of the internal jugular and subclavian veins behind the sternoclavicular joint. The left one is longer and crosses in front of the branches of the aortic arch.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the elbow, especially in semipronation.
Bundle of fibres joining the inferior colliculus with the medial geniculate body (auditory pathway).
Bundle of fibres joining the optic tract and the lateral geniculate body with the superior colliculus.
Bronchial tree: the main bronchi divide into lobar and segmental bronchi. The right main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical, so aspirated foreign bodies usually go to the right.
Skeletal muscle. It presses the cheek against the teeth; it keeps food between the dental arches and allows blowing.
Common tendon of the gastrocnemius and soleus, the thickest and strongest in the body. It inserts on the calcaneal tuberosity and transmits the force of plantar flexion.

Short bone of the tarsus. The seven tarsal bones form the posterior skeleton of the foot. It is the largest bone of the foot and forms the heel; the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon inserts on its tuberosity.
Short bone of the carpus. The eight carpal bones are arranged in two rows and form the skeleton of the wrist. Distal row; it is the largest carpal bone and articulates with the third metacarpal.
C-shaped nucleus of grey matter that follows the wall of the lateral ventricle. With the putamen it forms the striatum: movement planning, learning and motivation.
First visceral branch of the abdominal aorta (T12). It divides into the left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries: it supplies the stomach, liver, spleen, pancreas and duodenum.

concepts.n: Central canal of the spinal cord
concepts.d: Narrow canal, continuation of the fourth ventricle, running through the centre of the spinal cord. (The spinal cord itself is not represented in this model.)

Organ located in the posterior cranial fossa, behind the brainstem. It coordinates movement, balance and muscle tone, and takes part in motor learning. It contains more neurons than the rest of the brain.
Narrow canal of the midbrain joining the third and fourth ventricles. Its obstruction is a frequent cause of hydrocephalus.
Skeletal muscle. They stabilise and rotate the spine; proprioceptive function.

concepts.n: Choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle
concepts.d: Network of capillaries covered by ependymal epithelium that produces cerebrospinal fluid (≈500 ml/day).

Gyrus of the cerebral cortex (grey matter). It surrounds the corpus callosum on the medial surface of the hemisphere. Part of the limbic system: emotions, motivation, attention, pain and error monitoring.

Long bone shaped like an italic S that joins the upper limb to the trunk. It articulates medially with the sternum and laterally with the acromion of the scapula. It is the most frequently fractured bone.
Anterior part of the deltoid, the muscle that gives the shoulder its rounded shape.
Upper part of the pectoralis major, a large fan-shaped muscle of the anterior chest wall.
Skeletal muscle. It supports the pelvic viscera and flexes the coccyx.

Part of the large intestine between the caecum and the rectum: ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid. It absorbs water and electrolytes and forms the faeces. It has haustra, taeniae coli and omental appendices.
Fibres that cross between the posterior pillars of both fornices, connecting the two hippocampi.

It ascends the neck and, at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4), divides into the external carotid (face and neck) and internal carotid (brain and eye). At its bifurcation lies the carotid sinus, a blood pressure sensor.
Branch of the celiac trunk that supplies the liver, gallbladder, stomach (lesser and greater curvatures), duodenum and pancreas.
Terminal branch of the aorta (L4). It divides in front of the sacroiliac joint into the external and internal iliac arteries.
Formed by the union of the external and internal iliac veins. Both join at the level of L5 to form the inferior vena cava.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes and adducts the arm.
Wide vein in the posterior coronary groove that collects most of the venous blood of the heart and drains into the right atrium.
The largest commissure of the brain: about 200 million axons that connect the two cerebral hemispheres and allow information to be shared between them.
Two cylinders of erectile tissue on the dorsal side of the penis. When they fill with blood they produce the erection.
Cylinder of erectile tissue on the ventral side of the penis that surrounds the spongy urethra and ends in the glans.
Skeletal muscle. It pulls the eyebrow down and in (frowning).
Hyaline cartilages of the false ribs. They join one another and the seventh cartilage, forming the costal margin or arch.
Short bone of the tarsus. The seven tarsal bones form the posterior skeleton of the foot. Located on the lateral border of the foot; the tendon of the fibularis longus runs in its groove.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the thumb.
Skeletal muscle. It elevates the mandible and helps retract it.
Muscular duct of ≈45 cm that carries the sperm from the epididymis, through the inguinal canal and the pelvis, to the ejaculatory duct.
Skeletal muscle. It depresses the angle of the mouth (expression of sadness).
Skeletal muscle. It depresses and everts the lower lip.
Skeletal muscle. It pulls the septum down and dilates the nostril.
Continuation of the aortic arch: the thoracic part descends beside the spine, crosses the diaphragm (T12) and as the abdominal aorta bifurcates into the common iliac arteries at L4.
Upper part of the trapezius, a large flat triangular muscle of the nape and back.

Dome-shaped musculotendinous septum that separates the thorax from the abdomen. It is the main respiratory muscle; the inferior vena cava (T8), the oesophagus (T10) and the aorta (T12) pass through it.

concepts.n: Distal phalanx of the big toe (hallux)
concepts.d: Bone of the toes. They are shorter than those of the hand; the big toe has only two phalanges.

concepts.n: Distal phalanx of the fourth toe
concepts.d: Bone of the toes. They are shorter than those of the hand; the big toe has only two phalanges.

concepts.n: Distal phalanx of the index finger
concepts.d: Miniature long bone of the fingers. Terminal part of the digit; its tuberosity supports the pulp and the nail.

concepts.n: Distal phalanx of the little finger
concepts.d: Miniature long bone of the fingers. Terminal part of the digit; its tuberosity supports the pulp and the nail.

concepts.n: Distal phalanx of the fifth toe
concepts.d: Bone of the toes. They are shorter than those of the hand; the big toe has only two phalanges.

concepts.n: Distal phalanx of the middle finger
concepts.d: Miniature long bone of the fingers. Terminal part of the digit; its tuberosity supports the pulp and the nail.

concepts.n: Distal phalanx of the ring finger
concepts.d: Miniature long bone of the fingers. Terminal part of the digit; its tuberosity supports the pulp and the nail.

concepts.n: Distal phalanx of the second toe
concepts.d: Bone of the toes. They are shorter than those of the hand; the big toe has only two phalanges.

concepts.n: Distal phalanx of the third toe
concepts.d: Bone of the toes. They are shorter than those of the hand; the big toe has only two phalanges.
Miniature long bone of the fingers. Terminal part of the digit; its tuberosity supports the pulp and the nail.
First part of the small intestine (≈25 cm), C-shaped around the head of the pancreas. The common bile duct and the pancreatic duct open into its second part (ampulla of Vater).
Visible part of the outer ear, formed by elastic cartilage covered with skin (except the lobule). It collects sound waves and directs them to the external acoustic meatus.
False rib (vertebrochondral): its cartilage joins that of the rib above, forming the costal arch.
Thoracic vertebra: it has costal facets on the body and on the transverse processes to articulate with the ribs, and a long spinous process pointing downward.
Floating rib: its anterior end ends free in the muscles of the abdominal wall.

Thoracic vertebra: it has costal facets on the body and on the transverse processes to articulate with the ribs, and a long spinous process pointing downward. Its costal facets are complete and single; it no longer articulates with the transverse processes.
Highly coiled duct (≈6 m if unrolled) attached to the posterior border of the testis, where sperm mature and are stored.

Muscular tube of ≈25 cm that carries the food bolus from the pharynx to the stomach by peristaltic waves. It crosses the diaphragm at the level of T10. Its upper third has striated muscle and the lower two thirds, smooth muscle.
Unpaired, light bone located between the orbits. It forms part of the roof and walls of the nasal cavities; its cribriform plate lets the filaments of the olfactory nerve pass.
Its tendon of origin is the one most affected in lateral epicondylitis ("tennis elbow").
Skeletal muscle. It extends and abducts the wrist.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the little finger.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the fingers and the wrist.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the 2nd–4th fingers.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the fingers and dorsiflexes the foot.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the big toe.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the big toe and dorsiflexes the foot.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the index finger (pointing).
Skeletal muscle. It extends the thumb at the metacarpophalangeal joint.
Skeletal muscle. It extends all the joints of the thumb.
Ring of skeletal muscle under voluntary control that closes the anal canal.
It runs along the pelvic brim and, passing under the inguinal ligament, becomes the femoral artery, the main artery of the lower limb.
Continuation of the femoral vein above the inguinal ligament; it drains the lower limb.
Skeletal muscle. They elevate the ribs during inspiration.
The most superficial and largest of the broad muscles of the abdomen; its lower border forms the inguinal ligament.

Organ of vision, spherical, ≈24 mm in diameter. It has three layers: fibrous (sclera and cornea), vascular (choroid, ciliary body and iris) and inner (retina). The lens and the cornea focus light on the retina.
Bone of the thigh; it is the longest, heaviest and strongest bone in the body (≈1/4 of body height). Its head articulates with the acetabulum and its condyles with the tibia and the patella.
Lateral, slender bone of the leg. It bears hardly any weight, but gives attachment to muscles and its distal end forms the lateral malleolus, which stabilises the ankle.
Skeletal muscle. It everts the foot.
Skeletal muscle. It everts the foot, helps in plantar flexion and supports the transverse arch.
Skeletal muscle. Dorsiflexion and eversion of the foot.
Typical cervical vertebra: small body, transverse foramina through which the vertebral artery ascends (C1–C6) and a short spinous process, bifid in C3–C6.
Hyaline cartilage that joins the anterior end of the rib to the sternum. Its elasticity allows the thoracic cage to expand during breathing.

Lumbar vertebra: the largest, with a kidney-shaped, robust body adapted to bear the weight of the trunk. Its spinous processes are short and horizontal. It articulates with the sacrum at the lumbosacral joint; the L5–S1 disc is one of those most affected by herniation.
Long bone of the palm of the hand. Its base articulates with the carpus and its head with the proximal phalanx (knuckle). Metacarpal of the little finger.

Long bone of the forefoot. Its base articulates with the tarsus and its head with the proximal phalanx; the metatarsal heads rest on the ground during walking. Its tuberosity receives the tendon of the fibularis brevis.
True rib (vertebrosternal): it joins the sternum directly through its own costal cartilage.
Thoracic vertebra: it has costal facets on the body and on the transverse processes to articulate with the ribs, and a long spinous process pointing downward.
Hyaline cartilage that joins the anterior end of the rib to the sternum. Its elasticity allows the thoracic cage to expand during breathing.
Lumbar vertebra: the largest, with a kidney-shaped, robust body adapted to bear the weight of the trunk. Its spinous processes are short and horizontal.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the metatarsophalangeal joint and extends the interphalangeal joints.
Long bone of the palm of the hand. Its base articulates with the carpus and its head with the proximal phalanx (knuckle). Metacarpal of the thumb; the shortest and most robust, with great mobility.

Long bone of the forefoot. Its base articulates with the tarsus and its head with the proximal phalanx; the metatarsal heads rest on the ground during walking. It is the shortest and thickest; it bears the greatest load.
Skeletal muscle. It adducts the toe toward the axis of the second toe.
True rib (vertebrosternal): it joins the sternum directly through its own costal cartilage. It is the shortest, widest and flattest; the subclavian artery and vein cross its upper surface.

Thoracic vertebra: it has costal facets on the body and on the transverse processes to articulate with the ribs, and a long spinous process pointing downward. It articulates with the first rib and part of the second.
Skeletal muscle. It corrects the oblique pull of the flexor digitorum longus.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes and abducts the wrist.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the fifth toe.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the little finger.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the 2nd–5th fingers.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the 2nd–5th toes and helps in plantar flexion.
Skeletal muscle. Only flexor of the distal interphalangeal joints.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the big toe (push-off during walking).
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the thumb.

Fibrous band that crosses the palmar side of the carpus and turns the carpal groove into the carpal tunnel, through which the median nerve and the flexor tendons pass. Its compression causes carpal tunnel syndrome.
Arched bundle of fibres that is the main output pathway of the hippocampus; it ends mostly in the mammillary bodies. It takes part in memory circuits (Papez circuit).
Typical cervical vertebra: small body, transverse foramina through which the vertebral artery ascends (C1–C6) and a short spinous process, bifid in C3–C6.
Hyaline cartilage that joins the anterior end of the rib to the sternum. Its elasticity allows the thoracic cage to expand during breathing.
Lumbar vertebra: the largest, with a kidney-shaped, robust body adapted to bear the weight of the trunk. Its spinous processes are short and horizontal.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the metatarsophalangeal joint and extends the interphalangeal joints.
Long bone of the palm of the hand. Its base articulates with the carpus and its head with the proximal phalanx (knuckle). Metacarpal of the ring finger.
Long bone of the forefoot. Its base articulates with the tarsus and its head with the proximal phalanx; the metatarsal heads rest on the ground during walking.
True rib (vertebrosternal): it joins the sternum directly through its own costal cartilage.
Thoracic vertebra: it has costal facets on the body and on the transverse processes to articulate with the ribs, and a long spinous process pointing downward.
Rhomboid cavity between the brainstem and the cerebellum. Its openings (median and lateral) release cerebrospinal fluid into the subarachnoid space.
One of the three longitudinal bands of smooth muscle of the colon; it is visible on the anterior surface of the ascending and descending colon.
Unpaired bone that forms the forehead, the roof of the orbits and the anterior part of the cranial vault. It contains the frontal sinuses.
Skeletal muscle. It elevates the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead horizontally.
Gyrus of the cerebral cortex (grey matter). On the inferior surface of the hemisphere. It contains the fusiform face area and the visual word form area.
Pear-shaped sac under the liver that stores and concentrates bile (≈30–50 ml). It empties it into the duodenum after fatty meals under the action of cholecystokinin.

concepts.d: Skeletal muscle. It laterally rotates the thigh.

concepts.g: Lower limb: hip and gluteal region (lateral rotators)
concepts.d: Skeletal muscle. It laterally rotates the thigh.
Skeletal muscle. It pulls the hyoid forward and up; it depresses the mandible.
Fibrous mucosa that covers the alveolar part of the mandible and surrounds the neck of the teeth.
Fibrous mucosa that covers the alveolar processes of the maxilla and surrounds the neck of the teeth.
Expanded distal end of the corpus spongiosum; it contains the external urethral orifice and abundant sensory endings.
Medial part of the lentiform nucleus. It is the main output of the basal ganglia to the thalamus; its function is inhibitory.

concepts.g: Lower limb: hip and gluteal region
concepts.d: The bulkiest muscle in the body. It extends the hip and laterally rotates it.

concepts.g: Lower limb: hip and gluteal region
concepts.d: Its weakness produces the Trendelenburg sign (drop of the pelvis on the opposite side when standing on that leg).

concepts.g: Lower limb: hip and gluteal region
concepts.d: Skeletal muscle. It abducts and medially rotates the thigh; it stabilises the pelvis.
Skeletal muscle. It adducts the thigh and flexes the knee.
It ascends in the anterior interventricular groove alongside the anterior interventricular artery and drains into the coronary sinus.
Small nucleus of the epithalamus, next to the pineal gland. It takes part in the response to negative reward and aversion.
Short bone of the carpus. The eight carpal bones are arranged in two rows and form the skeleton of the wrist. Distal row; its hook bounds Guyon's canal, through which the ulnar nerve and artery pass.
Paired bone formed by the fusion of the ilium, ischium and pubis, which converge at the acetabulum, where the head of the femur sits. With the sacrum and coccyx it forms the bony pelvis.

Curved structure of the medial temporal lobe, in the floor of the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle. Essential for forming new declarative memories and for spatial memory; one of the first regions affected in Alzheimer's disease.
Skeletal muscle. It extends and adducts the wrist.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes and adducts the wrist.
Skeletal muscle. It pronates the forearm and flexes the elbow.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints and the wrist.
Long bone of the arm. Its head articulates with the scapula (shoulder) and its distal end with the radius and ulna (elbow). The radial nerve runs in its groove on the shaft.
U-shaped bone located in the neck at the level of C3. It is the only bone that does not articulate with any other: it is suspended by muscles and ligaments and serves as an anchor for the tongue.
Region of the diencephalon below the thalamus. It controls the autonomic nervous system and the pituitary gland, and regulates temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep and circadian rhythms.
Final part of the small intestine (distal ≈3/5). It absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts and contains Peyer's patches (lymphoid tissue). It opens into the caecum through the ileocecal valve.

Skeletal muscle. It supports the pelvic viscera.

concepts.g: Lower limb: hip and gluteal region
concepts.d: Lateral thickening of the fascia lata that extends from the iliac crest to the lateral condyle of the tibia (Gerdy's tubercle). It receives the tensor fasciae latae and the gluteus maximus and stabilises the hip and knee.
Eminence of the roof of the midbrain that is an obligatory relay of the auditory pathway and takes part in sound localisation.
It arises from the aorta at L3 and supplies the distal third of the transverse colon, the descending colon, the sigmoid and the upper rectum.
Paired, curved bone on the lateral wall of the nasal cavity. It increases the surface of the mucosa that warms and humidifies inspired air.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes and tilts the neck.
Gyrus of the cerebral cortex (grey matter). Part of the ventral visual pathway ("what"): recognition of objects and shapes.
The largest vein in the body. It forms at L5 by the union of the common iliac veins, ascends to the right of the aorta, crosses the diaphragm (T8) and drains into the right atrium.
Skeletal muscle. It laterally rotates the arm and stabilises the shoulder.

Fibrous band that extends from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. It is the thickened lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis and marks the boundary between abdomen and thigh.
Skeletal muscle. They act together with the internal intercostals.

Lobe of the cerebral cortex hidden in the depth of the lateral sulcus, covered by the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula. It processes taste, interoception (visceral sensations), pain and emotional awareness.
Short bone of the tarsus. The seven tarsal bones form the posterior skeleton of the foot. The smallest of the cuneiforms; it articulates with the second metatarsal.
Tendon that joins the anterior and posterior bellies of the digastric. It passes through the stylohyoid and is attached to the hyoid by a fibrous loop.
It supplies the pelvic viscera, the perineum, the gluteal region and the medial part of the thigh.
It drains the pelvic viscera, the perineum and the gluteal region.
Skeletal muscle. They lower the ribs during forced expiration.
It collects blood from the brain, face and neck. It arises at the jugular foramen and descends in the carotid sheath alongside the carotid artery and the vagus nerve.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes and rotates the trunk to the same side; it compresses the abdomen.
Fibrous sheet that joins the interosseous borders of the radius and ulna. It transmits forces from the radius to the ulna and gives origin to deep muscles of the forearm.
Fibrous sheet that joins the interosseous borders of the tibia and fibula. It separates the anterior and posterior compartments of the leg and gives origin to muscles.
Depression between the two cerebral peduncles, on the anterior surface of the midbrain, from which the oculomotor nerve (III) emerges.
Opening that connects each lateral ventricle with the third ventricle.

Second part of the small intestine (proximal ≈2/5 of the jejunoileum). It has tall, abundant circular folds and is the main site of nutrient absorption.

Bean-shaped retroperitoneal organ (≈11 cm) located between T12 and L3; the right one is slightly lower because of the liver. It filters ≈180 L of plasma per day through ≈1 million nephrons and produces 1–2 L of urine. It also secretes renin and erythropoietin.
Musculomembranous folds that surround the mouth opening, formed by the orbicularis oris muscle covered by skin and mucosa. Its red zone (vermilion) has a thin, highly vascularised epithelium.
Paired bone, the smallest of the face, on the medial wall of the orbit. It contains the fossa for the lacrimal sac.
Thin sheet that forms the anterior wall of the third ventricle. It contains the vascular organ, sensitive to blood osmolarity (thirst).
Short bone of the tarsus. The seven tarsal bones form the posterior skeleton of the foot. It articulates with the third metatarsal and the cuboid.
Thalamic nucleus that receives the optic tract and sends the optic radiation to the visual cortex. It is the relay of the visual pathway.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the big toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint.
Skeletal muscle. Plantar flexion of the foot and flexion of the knee.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the elbow.
C-shaped cavity inside each hemisphere, filled with cerebrospinal fluid. It communicates with the third ventricle through the interventricular foramen.
The broadest muscle in the body. It extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm.
Skeletal muscle. It elevates the angle of the mouth.
Skeletal muscle. It elevates and everts the upper lip.
Skeletal muscle. It elevates the upper lip and dilates the nostril.
Skeletal muscle. It elevates the scapula and tilts the neck.

Fibrous raphe of the anterior midline of the abdomen, from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis, formed by the interlacing of the aponeuroses of the broad muscles of the abdomen. It contains the umbilicus.

The largest gland in the body (≈1.5 kg), located in the right hypochondrium under the diaphragm. It produces bile, metabolises nutrients and drugs, synthesises plasma proteins and stores glycogen. It receives blood from the hepatic artery and the portal vein.
Primary lymphoid organ of the anterior mediastinum, formed by two lobes. T lymphocytes mature in it. It is large in childhood and is progressively replaced by fat in adults (involution).
Lateral head of the biceps brachii. Its tendon crosses the shoulder joint through the intertubercular groove.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the knee and extends the hip; it laterally rotates the leg.
Head of the triceps brachii, the only muscle of the posterior compartment of the arm and the main extensor of the elbow.
The longest ligament of the sole of the foot: it runs from the plantar surface of the calcaneus to the cuboid and the bases of metatarsals 2–5. It maintains the lateral longitudinal arch.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the head and turns it to the same side.
Skeletal muscle. It extends and laterally tilts the neck.
Skeletal muscle. It extends and laterally tilts the spine.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the head.

The smallest tooth of the permanent dentition; cutting crown and a single root. Teeth are part of the digestive system (oral cavity). Adults have 32 permanent teeth; in this model the third molars (wisdom teeth) are missing. They are made of enamel, dentin, pulp and cementum.

Molar with five cusps and two roots (mesial and distal). It erupts at about 6 years of age. Teeth are part of the digestive system (oral cavity). Adults have 32 permanent teeth; in this model the third molars (wisdom teeth) are missing. They are made of enamel, dentin, pulp and cementum.

Premolar with one dominant buccal cusp and a small lingual one; one root. Teeth are part of the digestive system (oral cavity). Adults have 32 permanent teeth; in this model the third molars (wisdom teeth) are missing. They are made of enamel, dentin, pulp and cementum.
Skeletal muscle. It protrudes the mandible and starts opening the mouth; lateral movements.

Cutting tooth with a single root, somewhat larger than the lower central incisor. Teeth are part of the digestive system (oral cavity). Adults have 32 permanent teeth; in this model the third molars (wisdom teeth) are missing. They are made of enamel, dentin, pulp and cementum.

Molar with four cusps and two roots. It erupts at about 12 years of age. Teeth are part of the digestive system (oral cavity). Adults have 32 permanent teeth; in this model the third molars (wisdom teeth) are missing. They are made of enamel, dentin, pulp and cementum.

Premolar with two or three cusps; one root. Teeth are part of the digestive system (oral cavity). Adults have 32 permanent teeth; in this model the third molars (wisdom teeth) are missing. They are made of enamel, dentin, pulp and cementum.

Tooth with a pointed cusp that tears food; a single long root. Teeth are part of the digestive system (oral cavity). Adults have 32 permanent teeth; in this model the third molars (wisdom teeth) are missing. They are made of enamel, dentin, pulp and cementum.
Skeletal muscle. They stabilise and rotate the spine; proprioceptive function.
Short bone of the carpus. The eight carpal bones are arranged in two rows and form the skeleton of the wrist. Proximal row; it is the carpal bone that dislocates most frequently.
Pair of small rounded eminences at the base of the hypothalamus. They receive the fornix and are part of the memory circuit; they are damaged in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.
The only movable bone of the skull and the strongest of the face. It houses the lower teeth and articulates with the temporal bones at the temporomandibular joints.
Upper part of the sternum. It articulates with the clavicles and the first costal cartilage; its junction with the body forms the sternal angle (of Louis), at the level of the second rib.
Paired bone that forms the upper jaw, part of the hard palate, the floor of the orbit and the lateral wall of the nasal cavities. It houses the upper teeth and the maxillary sinus.
Short bone of the tarsus. The seven tarsal bones form the posterior skeleton of the foot. The largest of the three cuneiforms; it articulates with the first metatarsal.
Thalamic nucleus that relays the auditory pathway: it receives fibres from the inferior colliculus and projects to the auditory cortex.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the big toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint.
Medial head of the "twins" (gastrocnemius), which form the bulge of the calf.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the elbow.
Skeletal muscle. It elevates the mandible and, together with the lateral pterygoid, produces lateral movements.

Lower part of the brainstem, continuing with the spinal cord at the foramen magnum. It houses vital cardiovascular and respiratory centres and the nuclei of cranial nerves IX to XII; the pyramids decussate in it.
Skeletal muscle. It elevates and protrudes the lower lip; it wrinkles the skin of the chin.
Taenia of the colon located on the line of attachment of the mesocolon.
Upper part of the brainstem. It contains the substantia nigra, the red nucleus and the nuclei of cranial nerves III and IV; it takes part in eye movements and motor control.
It runs in the posterior interventricular groove and drains into the coronary sinus.
Gyrus of the cerebral cortex (grey matter). It includes the frontal eye field (voluntary eye movements) and part of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (planning, working memory).

concepts.n: Middle phalanx of the fourth toe
concepts.d: Bone of the toes. They are shorter than those of the hand; the big toe has only two phalanges.

concepts.n: Middle phalanx of the index finger
concepts.d: Miniature long bone of the fingers. Located between the proximal and distal phalanges; the thumb has none.

concepts.n: Middle phalanx of the little finger
concepts.d: Miniature long bone of the fingers. Located between the proximal and distal phalanges; the thumb has none.

concepts.n: Middle phalanx of the fifth toe
concepts.d: Bone of the toes. They are shorter than those of the hand; the big toe has only two phalanges.

concepts.n: Middle phalanx of the middle finger
concepts.d: Miniature long bone of the fingers. Located between the proximal and distal phalanges; the thumb has none.

concepts.n: Middle phalanx of the ring finger
concepts.d: Miniature long bone of the fingers. Located between the proximal and distal phalanges; the thumb has none.

concepts.n: Middle phalanx of the second toe
concepts.d: Bone of the toes. They are shorter than those of the hand; the big toe has only two phalanges.

concepts.n: Middle phalanx of the third toe
concepts.d: Bone of the toes. They are shorter than those of the hand; the big toe has only two phalanges.
Gyrus of the cerebral cortex (grey matter). It takes part in the recognition of words and meanings, and in the perception of visual motion (area MT/V5 in its posterior part).
Left atrioventricular valve, with two cusps. It prevents the backflow of blood from the left ventricle to the left atrium during systole.
Deep muscle formed by short fascicles. It is a key segmental stabiliser of the lumbar spine.
Skeletal muscle. It forms the floor of the mouth; it elevates the hyoid and the tongue when swallowing.
Paired, small, elongated bone that forms the bony bridge of the nose.
Skeletal muscle. It compresses the nostril (transverse part) or dilates it (alar part).

Short bone of the tarsus. The seven tarsal bones form the posterior skeleton of the foot. Located on the medial side, between the talus and the three cuneiforms; it is the keystone of the medial longitudinal arch.
False rib (vertebrochondral): its cartilage joins that of the rib above, forming the costal arch.
Thoracic vertebra: it has costal facets on the body and on the transverse processes to articulate with the ribs, and a long spinous process pointing downward.
Skeletal muscle. It adducts the big toe; it supports the transverse arch.
Skeletal muscle. It adducts the thumb.
Skeletal muscle. It turns the atlas (and the head) to the same side.
Skeletal muscle. It extends and laterally tilts the head.

concepts.g: Lower limb: hip and gluteal region (lateral rotators)
concepts.d: Skeletal muscle. It laterally rotates the thigh.

concepts.g: Lower limb: hip and gluteal region (lateral rotators)
concepts.d: Skeletal muscle. It laterally rotates the thigh and stabilises the hip.
Unpaired bone of the posterior and lower part of the skull. It has the foramen magnum, through which the brain continues into the spinal cord, and the condyles that articulate with the atlas.
Posterior lobe of the cerebral hemisphere. It contains the primary visual cortex (V1, Brodmann area 17) around the calcarine sulcus and the visual association areas.
Skeletal muscle. It pulls the scalp backward.
Taenia of the colon to which the greater omentum attaches on the transverse colon.
Digastric muscle with an intermediate tendon attached to the clavicle by a fascial expansion. It depresses and fixes the hyoid.
Skeletal muscle. It pulls the fifth metatarsal (inconstant).
Skeletal muscle. It brings the fifth metacarpal forward (opposition).
Skeletal muscle. It opposes the thumb (brings it toward the palm to meet the other fingers).
X-shaped structure where the fibres from the nasal halves of both retinas cross. It lies just above the pituitary gland, so pituitary tumours can alter the visual field (bitemporal hemianopia).
Second cranial nerve. Formed by ≈1.2 million axons of the retinal ganglion cells; it carries visual information from the eye to the optic chiasm.
Continuation of the optic pathway from the chiasm to the lateral geniculate body. Each tract carries information from the opposite visual hemifield.
Skeletal muscle. It closes and protrudes the lips (whistling, kissing).

Gyrus of the cerebral cortex (grey matter). Inferior surface of the frontal lobe, above the roof of the orbits. Orbitofrontal cortex: decision-making, reward evaluation and control of social behaviour. The olfactory sulcus separates the gyrus rectus from the orbital gyri.
Skeletal muscle. It closes the eyelids tightly (forced wink).
Paired L-shaped bone that forms the posterior part of the hard palate and part of the lateral wall of the nasal cavities.
Inconstant muscle (absent in ≈15 % of people); its tendon is often used as a graft.
Skeletal muscle. It gently closes the eyelids (blinking and sleep).
Elongated retroperitoneal gland behind the stomach. Its exocrine part secretes digestive enzymes into the duodenum; its islets of Langerhans (endocrine) produce insulin and glucagon.
It runs through the pancreas from tail to head and joins the common bile duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens at the major duodenal papilla.

concepts.n: Papillary muscle of the left ventricle
concepts.d: Conical projection of the ventricular myocardium attached to the cusps by the chordae tendineae. By contracting in systole it prevents the atrioventricular valve cusps from bulging back into the atrium.

Gyrus of the cerebral cortex (grey matter). Part of the limbic system. Its anterior part (entorhinal cortex and uncus) is the main input pathway to the hippocampus; essential for memory and spatial orientation.
Paired, quadrilateral bone that forms most of the roof and lateral walls of the skull. The two parietal bones meet at the sagittal suture.
The largest sesamoid bone in the body, embedded in the quadriceps tendon. It protects the knee and increases the lever arm of the quadriceps in extension.
Skeletal muscle. It adducts and flexes the thigh.
Skeletal muscle. It depresses and protracts the scapula; it elevates the ribs if the scapula is fixed.
Anterior column of the midbrain formed by the base of the peduncle, which contains the descending corticospinal and corticonuclear fibres.
Small pine cone–shaped gland of the epithalamus, located behind the third ventricle. It secretes melatonin in darkness and regulates circadian rhythms.

concepts.g: Lower limb: hip and gluteal region (lateral rotators)
concepts.d: Key landmark of the gluteal region: the sciatic nerve usually leaves the pelvis below it.
Short bone of the carpus. The eight carpal bones are arranged in two rows and form the skeleton of the wrist. Proximal row; it is a sesamoid bone within the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris.

Gland of ≈0.5 g housed in the sella turcica of the sphenoid and connected to the hypothalamus by the pituitary stalk. It regulates other glands: the adenohypophysis secretes GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and prolactin; the neurohypophysis releases oxytocin and ADH.
Small muscle with a very long, thin tendon; inconstant.
Skeletal muscle. It tenses the skin of the neck and depresses the lower lip and the mandible.
Middle part of the brainstem. It connects the cortex with the cerebellum and contains respiratory centres and the nuclei of cranial nerves V, VI, VII and VIII.
Skeletal muscle. It "unlocks" the extended knee by laterally rotating the femur.

Gyrus of the cerebral cortex (grey matter). Primary somatosensory cortex (areas 3, 1 and 2): it receives touch, pain, temperature and proprioception from the opposite side of the body (sensory homunculus).
Skeletal muscle. It elevates and retracts the hyoid during swallowing.
Bundle of fibres that crosses the midline above the cerebral aqueduct; it takes part in the consensual pupillary light reflex.
Gyrus of the cerebral cortex (grey matter). In the dominant hemisphere it contains Wernicke's area, essential for language comprehension.

Gyrus of the cerebral cortex (grey matter). Primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4): it originates voluntary motor commands for the opposite side of the body, with a somatotopic representation (motor homunculus).
Skeletal muscle. It lowers the medial end of the eyebrows and produces transverse wrinkles at the root of the nose.
Skeletal muscle. Main pronator of the forearm.
Walnut-sized gland below the bladder, crossed by the urethra. It produces ≈20–30 % of the semen. Its growth with age (benign hyperplasia) can make urination difficult.

concepts.n: Proximal phalanx of the big toe (hallux)
concepts.d: Bone of the toes. They are shorter than those of the hand; the big toe has only two phalanges.

concepts.n: Proximal phalanx of the fourth toe
concepts.d: Bone of the toes. They are shorter than those of the hand; the big toe has only two phalanges.

concepts.n: Proximal phalanx of the index finger
concepts.d: Miniature long bone of the fingers. It articulates with the head of the metacarpal (metacarpophalangeal joint).

concepts.n: Proximal phalanx of the little finger
concepts.d: Miniature long bone of the fingers. It articulates with the head of the metacarpal (metacarpophalangeal joint).

concepts.n: Proximal phalanx of the fifth toe
concepts.d: Bone of the toes. They are shorter than those of the hand; the big toe has only two phalanges.

concepts.n: Proximal phalanx of the middle finger
concepts.d: Miniature long bone of the fingers. It articulates with the head of the metacarpal (metacarpophalangeal joint).

concepts.n: Proximal phalanx of the ring finger
concepts.d: Miniature long bone of the fingers. It articulates with the head of the metacarpal (metacarpophalangeal joint).

concepts.n: Proximal phalanx of the second toe
concepts.d: Bone of the toes. They are shorter than those of the hand; the big toe has only two phalanges.

concepts.n: Proximal phalanx of the third toe
concepts.d: Bone of the toes. They are shorter than those of the hand; the big toe has only two phalanges.
Miniature long bone of the fingers. It articulates with the head of the metacarpal (metacarpophalangeal joint).

concepts.g: Lower limb: hip and gluteal region
concepts.d: Long muscle of the posterior abdominal wall; with the iliacus it forms the iliopsoas, the most powerful hip flexor.
Part of the levator ani, the main component of the pelvic diaphragm.
Skeletal muscle. It maintains the anorectal angle; essential for faecal continence.

They carry oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. The pulmonary trunk divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries below the aortic arch. They are the only arteries in the adult that carry deoxygenated blood.
Semilunar valve with three cusps located between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk. It prevents backflow into the ventricle during diastole.
Normally four (two per lung). They carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. They are the only veins in the adult that carry oxygenated blood.

Lateral part of the lentiform nucleus. With the caudate it forms the striatum, which receives information from the cortex and regulates movement. Affected in Parkinson's disease by the loss of dopamine.
Small triangular, inconstant muscle (absent in ≈20 % of people), located in front of the rectus abdominis.

concepts.g: Lower limb: hip and gluteal region (lateral rotators)
concepts.d: Skeletal muscle. It laterally rotates the thigh.
Skeletal muscle. It laterally tilts the trunk and fixes the twelfth rib during inspiration.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints.
Lateral bone of the forearm (thumb side). It rotates around the ulna in pronation and supination. Its distal end forms most of the wrist joint.
Final part of the large intestine (≈12–15 cm), between the sigmoid colon (S3) and the anal canal. It temporarily stores faeces.
Long, flat muscle enclosed in the rectus sheath; its tendinous intersections give the "six-pack" look. It flexes the trunk.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the head at the atlanto-occipital joint.
Skeletal muscle. It laterally tilts the head.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the head and turns it to the same side.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the head.
The only head of the quadriceps that crosses the hip. It extends the knee and flexes the hip.
It arises from the aorta at L1–L2. The kidneys receive ≈20 % of the cardiac output. The right one is longer and passes behind the inferior vena cava.
It drains the kidney into the inferior vena cava. The left one is longer and crosses in front of the aorta, below the superior mesenteric artery.
Skeletal muscle. It retracts and elevates the scapula; it fixes it to the chest wall.
Skeletal muscle. It retracts and elevates the scapula.
Skeletal muscle. It pulls the angle of the mouth laterally.
Triangular bone formed by the fusion of the five sacral vertebrae. It wedges between the two hip bones at the sacroiliac joints and transmits the weight of the trunk to the pelvis.
The longest muscle in the body. It crosses the thigh diagonally and acts on the hip and knee.
Deep muscle of the neck. The subclavian artery passes behind it and the subclavian vein in front of it.
Skeletal muscle. It elevates the first rib; it tilts the neck.
Skeletal muscle. It elevates the second rib; it tilts the neck.

Short bone of the carpus. The eight carpal bones are arranged in two rows and form the skeleton of the wrist. The scaphoid (proximal row) is the one fractured most frequently; its retrograde blood supply favours necrosis after fracture.
Flat, triangular bone of the posterior part of the thorax. Its glenoid cavity articulates with the head of the humerus to form the shoulder; the spine ends in the acromion.
Hyaline cartilage that joins the anterior end of the rib to the sternum. Its elasticity allows the thoracic cage to expand during breathing.
Lumbar vertebra: the largest, with a kidney-shaped, robust body adapted to bear the weight of the trunk. Its spinous processes are short and horizontal.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the metatarsophalangeal joint and extends the interphalangeal joints.
Long bone of the palm of the hand. Its base articulates with the carpus and its head with the proximal phalanx (knuckle). Metacarpal of the index finger; the longest.

Long bone of the forefoot. Its base articulates with the tarsus and its head with the proximal phalanx; the metatarsal heads rest on the ground during walking. It is the longest; frequent in stress fractures.
Skeletal muscle. It adducts the toe toward the axis of the second toe.
True rib (vertebrosternal): it joins the sternum directly through its own costal cartilage.
Thoracic vertebra: it has costal facets on the body and on the transverse processes to articulate with the ribs, and a long spinous process pointing downward.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the knee, extends the hip and medially rotates the leg.
Tubular gland located behind the bladder. It provides ≈60–70 % of the semen volume, a fructose-rich fluid that nourishes the sperm.
Skeletal muscle. Main extensor of the head.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the neck and turns it to the opposite side.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the spine and turns it to the opposite side.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the knee, extends the hip and medially rotates the leg.

concepts.n: Septal papillary muscle of the right ventricle
concepts.d: Conical projection of the ventricular myocardium attached to the cusps by the chordae tendineae. By contracting in systole it prevents the atrioventricular valve cusps from bulging back into the atrium.
Thin double sheet that separates the anterior horns of the lateral ventricles, between the corpus callosum and the fornix.
Its paralysis produces a "winged scapula". It protracts and rotates the scapula.
Skeletal muscle. It lowers the lower ribs.
Skeletal muscle. It elevates the ribs (an inspiratory function is attributed to it).
Small bones embedded in the tendons of the flexor hallucis brevis, under the head of the first metatarsal. They protect the tendon and improve its leverage.
Small veins of the anterior surface of the right ventricle that open directly into the right atrium.
Skeletal muscle. Lateral tilt and stabilisation of the neck.
Skeletal muscle. They abduct the toes away from the axis of the second toe.
Skeletal muscle. They abduct the fingers away from the axis of the middle finger (DAB).
Thick hairs located on the supraorbital margin. They divert sweat and water away from the eyes and take part in facial expression.
Set of terminal hairs of the scalp. Each hair arises from a hair follicle in the dermis; it is made of hard keratin and grows about 1 cm per month.
Skeletal muscle. They extend the neck and stabilise it.
Skeletal muscle. They extend and stabilise the lumbar spine.
Skeletal muscle. They extend and stabilise the spine.
Skeletal muscle. Lateral tilt of the lumbar spine.
Skeletal muscle. They elevate the ribs; they tilt the spine.
Skeletal muscle. They elevate the ribs; they tilt the spine.
Skeletal muscle. They flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints.
Skeletal muscle. Lateral tilt and lumbar stabilisation.
Hyaline cartilages that form the skeleton of the movable part of the nose: greater alar, lateral and septal cartilages.
Skeletal muscle. They adduct the fingers toward the axis of the middle finger (PAD).
Skeletal muscle. Lateral tilt and stabilisation of the neck.
Terminal hair of the pubic region, which appears at puberty under the action of androgens. It is a secondary sexual characteristic.
Vertebra prominens: its long, non-bifid spinous process is easily palpable at the base of the neck and serves as a clinical landmark.
Hyaline cartilage that joins the anterior end of the rib to the sternum. Its elasticity allows the thoracic cage to expand during breathing.
True rib (vertebrosternal): it joins the sternum directly through its own costal cartilage.
Thoracic vertebra: it has costal facets on the body and on the transverse processes to articulate with the ribs, and a long spinous process pointing downward.
Skeletal muscle. Powerful supinator of the forearm and flexor of the elbow.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the knee and laterally rotates the leg.
Typical cervical vertebra: small body, transverse foramina through which the vertebral artery ascends (C1–C6) and a short spinous process, bifid in C3–C6.
Hyaline cartilage that joins the anterior end of the rib to the sternum. Its elasticity allows the thoracic cage to expand during breathing.
True rib (vertebrosternal): it joins the sternum directly through its own costal cartilage.
Thoracic vertebra: it has costal facets on the body and on the transverse processes to articulate with the ribs, and a long spinous process pointing downward.

Organ that covers the entire body surface (≈1.8 m² and ≈4 kg in adults). It consists of the epidermis (keratinised stratified squamous epithelium), the dermis (connective tissue with vessels, nerves, hair follicles and glands) and rests on the hypodermis or subcutaneous tissue.
Broad, flat muscle under the gastrocnemius. Its contraction drives venous blood toward the heart ("muscle pump").
Unpaired butterfly-shaped bone located in the centre of the base of the skull. Its sella turcica houses the pituitary gland and it articulates with all the other bones of the neurocranium.
Skeletal muscle. It extends and laterally rotates the arm.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the neck.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the thoracic spine.

Lymphoid organ located in the left hypochondrium, under ribs 9–11. Its red pulp filters the blood and removes aged red blood cells; its white pulp generates immune responses against blood-borne pathogens.
The thickest branch of the celiac trunk; it runs tortuously along the upper border of the pancreas to the spleen.
It drains the spleen and part of the pancreas and stomach; after receiving the inferior mesenteric vein it joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the portal vein.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the head; unilaterally it turns it to the same side.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the neck and turns it to the same side.
Skeletal muscle. Unilateral: it tilts the head to the same side and turns it to the opposite side. Bilateral: it flexes the neck; accessory inspiratory muscle.
Skeletal muscle. It adducts and medially rotates the arm; it extends it from flexion.
Skeletal muscle. It lowers the hyoid after swallowing.
Skeletal muscle. It lowers the larynx.
J-shaped dilation of the digestive tract located in the epigastrium and left hypochondrium. It stores food and partially digests it with hydrochloric acid and pepsin, turning it into chyme.
Bundle of fibres on the medial surface of the thalamus that carries information from the septal area to the habenular nuclei.
Bundle of fibres that runs alongside the caudate nucleus and connects the amygdala with the hypothalamus and the septal area.
Skeletal muscle. It elevates and retracts the hyoid.

Main artery of the upper limb. It passes between the scalenus anterior and medius over the first rib and continues as the axillary artery. It gives off the vertebral artery, which supplies the posterior brain.
Continuation of the axillary vein. It passes in front of the scalenus anterior, over the first rib, and joins the internal jugular vein. It is a common route for central venous access.
Skeletal muscle. It fixes and lowers the clavicle.
Skeletal muscle. It medially rotates the arm and stabilises the shoulder.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the thumb at the metacarpophalangeal joint.
Superficial portion, the bulkiest, of the masseter, one of the most powerful muscles of the body relative to its size.
Eminence of the roof of the midbrain that coordinates eye and head movements toward visual stimuli (visual reflexes).
Gyrus of the cerebral cortex (grey matter). It contains the supplementary motor area and takes part in executive functions, self-awareness and working memory.
It arises from the aorta at L1 and supplies the small intestine (from the second part of the duodenum), the caecum, the ascending colon and 2/3 of the transverse colon.
It drains the small intestine, the caecum and the ascending and transverse colon. With the splenic vein it forms the portal vein, which carries absorbed nutrients to the liver.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the neck.

Gyrus of the cerebral cortex (grey matter). It integrates visual and somatosensory information to orient the body in space and guide movements. The precuneus, on the medial surface, takes part in episodic memory and self-awareness.
Formed by the union of the two brachiocephalic veins. It collects blood from the head, neck, upper limbs and thorax and drains into the right atrium.
Skeletal muscle. It supinates the forearm.

Gyrus of the cerebral cortex (grey matter). It surrounds the end of the lateral sulcus. It takes part in spatial perception, praxis and, in the dominant hemisphere, in the phonological processing of language.
Part of the rotator cuff; its tendon is the one most frequently injured in the shoulder.

Short bone of the tarsus. The seven tarsal bones form the posterior skeleton of the foot. It transmits the weight of the tibia to the rest of the foot; it has no muscle attachments and is largely covered by articular cartilage.
Paired bone of the lateral wall and base of the skull. Its petrous part houses the middle and inner ear and it articulates with the mandible at the temporomandibular joint.
Skeletal muscle. It elevates the mandible; its posterior fibres retract it.
Skeletal muscle. It tenses the scalp and elevates the auricle.

concepts.n: Tendinous arch of the levator ani
concepts.d: Thickening of the fascia of the obturator internus that extends from the pubis to the ischial spine and gives origin to part of the levator ani.

concepts.g: Lower limb: hip and gluteal region
concepts.d: Skeletal muscle. It abducts, flexes and medially rotates the thigh; it stabilises the knee in extension.
False rib (vertebrochondral): its cartilage joins that of the rib above, forming the costal arch.
Thoracic vertebra: it has costal facets on the body and on the transverse processes to articulate with the ribs, and a long spinous process pointing downward.
Skeletal muscle. It adducts, extends and medially rotates the arm.
Skeletal muscle. It laterally rotates the arm and stabilises the shoulder.
Male gonad, ovoid (≈4–5 cm), housed in the scrotum. Its seminiferous tubules produce sperm and the Leydig cells produce testosterone.

Ovoid mass of grey matter on each side of the third ventricle. It is the great relay station: almost all sensory information (except smell) passes through it before reaching the cortex. It also regulates wakefulness and attention.
Typical cervical vertebra: small body, transverse foramina through which the vertebral artery ascends (C1–C6) and a short spinous process, bifid in C3–C6.
Hyaline cartilage that joins the anterior end of the rib to the sternum. Its elasticity allows the thoracic cage to expand during breathing.
Lumbar vertebra: the largest, with a kidney-shaped, robust body adapted to bear the weight of the trunk. Its spinous processes are short and horizontal.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the metatarsophalangeal joint and extends the interphalangeal joints.
Long bone of the palm of the hand. Its base articulates with the carpus and its head with the proximal phalanx (knuckle). Metacarpal of the middle finger; it has the styloid process at its base.
Long bone of the forefoot. Its base articulates with the tarsus and its head with the proximal phalanx; the metatarsal heads rest on the ground during walking.
Skeletal muscle. It adducts the toe toward the axis of the second toe.
True rib (vertebrosternal): it joins the sternum directly through its own costal cartilage.
Thoracic vertebra: it has costal facets on the body and on the transverse processes to articulate with the ribs, and a long spinous process pointing downward.
Narrow, medial cavity between the two thalami, filled with cerebrospinal fluid. It communicates with the lateral ventricles and, through the aqueduct, with the fourth ventricle.
Skeletal muscle. They stabilise and rotate the spine; proprioceptive function.
Skeletal muscle. It lowers the hyoid or elevates the larynx if the hyoid is fixed.

The largest cartilage of the larynx. Its two laminae join at the front forming the laryngeal prominence ("Adam's apple"), more marked in males. It protects the vocal cords, which attach to its inner surface.
Medial and main bone of the leg, which bears body weight. Its anterior border is subcutaneous and its distal end forms the medial malleolus.
Its paralysis causes "foot drop". It dorsiflexes and inverts the foot.
Skeletal muscle. Inversion and plantar flexion of the foot; it supports the medial longitudinal arch.
Tube of ≈10–12 cm running from the larynx (C6) to the carina (T4–T5), where it divides into the two main bronchi. It is supported by 16–20 C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, open at the back.
Skeletal muscle. It adducts the big toe; it supports the transverse arch.
Skeletal muscle. It adducts the thumb (lateral pinch).
Skeletal muscle. It retracts the scapula (brings it toward the spine).
Skeletal muscle. It compresses the abdominal contents and stabilises the lumbar spine.
Skeletal muscle. It lowers the costal cartilages (expiration).

Short bone of the carpus. The eight carpal bones are arranged in two rows and form the skeleton of the wrist. Distal row; it articulates in a saddle joint with the first metacarpal, which allows opposition of the thumb.
Short bone of the carpus. The eight carpal bones are arranged in two rows and form the skeleton of the wrist. Distal row; the smallest of the row, it articulates with the second metacarpal.
Right atrioventricular valve, with three cusps. It prevents the backflow of blood from the right ventricle to the right atrium during systole.
Short bone of the carpus. The eight carpal bones are arranged in two rows and form the skeleton of the wrist. Proximal row; it articulates with the pisiform on its palmar surface.
Eminence of grey matter at the base of the hypothalamus, between the optic chiasm and the mammillary bodies; the pituitary stalk arises from it.
Floating rib: its anterior end ends free in the muscles of the abdominal wall.

Thoracic vertebra: it has costal facets on the body and on the transverse processes to articulate with the ribs, and a long spinous process pointing downward. Its costal facets are complete and single; it no longer articulates with the transverse processes.
Medial bone of the forearm. Its olecranon forms the point of the elbow and its trochlear notch articulates with the humerus.
Skeletal muscle. It extends and adducts the wrist.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes and adducts the wrist.
Deep head of the pronator teres; the median nerve passes between the two heads.

Tooth with a shovel-shaped crown and a single root; it cuts food. Teeth are part of the digestive system (oral cavity). Adults have 32 permanent teeth; in this model the third molars (wisdom teeth) are missing. They are made of enamel, dentin, pulp and cementum.

Large molar with four cusps and three roots; it grinds food. It erupts at about 6 years of age. Teeth are part of the digestive system (oral cavity). Adults have 32 permanent teeth; in this model the third molars (wisdom teeth) are missing. They are made of enamel, dentin, pulp and cementum.

Tooth with two cusps that crushes food; it usually has two roots. Teeth are part of the digestive system (oral cavity). Adults have 32 permanent teeth; in this model the third molars (wisdom teeth) are missing. They are made of enamel, dentin, pulp and cementum.
Skeletal muscle. It stabilises the articular disc when the mouth closes.

Cutting tooth, smaller than the central incisor, with a single root. Teeth are part of the digestive system (oral cavity). Adults have 32 permanent teeth; in this model the third molars (wisdom teeth) are missing. They are made of enamel, dentin, pulp and cementum.

Molar with three or four cusps and three roots. It erupts at about 12 years of age. Teeth are part of the digestive system (oral cavity). Adults have 32 permanent teeth; in this model the third molars (wisdom teeth) are missing. They are made of enamel, dentin, pulp and cementum.

Tooth with two cusps that crushes food; it usually has one root. Teeth are part of the digestive system (oral cavity). Adults have 32 permanent teeth; in this model the third molars (wisdom teeth) are missing. They are made of enamel, dentin, pulp and cementum.

Tooth with a pointed cusp that tears food. It has the longest root of the dentition. Teeth are part of the digestive system (oral cavity). Adults have 32 permanent teeth; in this model the third molars (wisdom teeth) are missing. They are made of enamel, dentin, pulp and cementum.
Muscular duct of ≈25 cm that carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder by peristalsis. It has three narrowings where stones can lodge.
Duct that carries urine from the bladder to the outside. In males (≈20 cm) it is also the pathway of semen and has prostatic, membranous and spongy portions.
Hollow muscular organ located in the pelvis, behind the pubic symphysis. It stores urine; its wall (detrusor muscle) contracts during urination.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the knee.
The bulkiest head of the quadriceps.
Skeletal muscle. It extends the knee; its oblique fibres stabilise the patella.
Skeletal muscle. It flexes the neck.
Unpaired, flat bone that forms the posteroinferior part of the nasal septum.

Fist-sized hollow muscular organ located in the middle mediastinum. It has four chambers (two atria and two ventricles). Its wall consists of endocardium, myocardium and epicardium. It beats about 100,000 times a day.

concepts.n: White matter of the cerebral hemispheres
concepts.d: Mass of myelinated axons located under the cortex. It contains association fibres (joining areas of the same hemisphere), commissural fibres (joining both hemispheres) and projection fibres (joining the cortex with lower structures).
Small, lower end of the sternum. It is cartilaginous in young people and ossifies with age; the linea alba inserts on it.
Paired bone that forms the cheekbone and part of the lateral wall of the orbit. With the zygomatic process of the temporal bone it forms the zygomatic arch.
Skeletal muscle. It pulls the angle of the mouth up and back (smile).
Skeletal muscle. It elevates the upper lip.
